opus-5.5.text:
I think this goes back to a very basic question: what is a "state," really? When people talk about world models, there's a tendency to equate the state with the raw observation: every pixel, every frame, every detail of the sensory input. But that's not what a state should be. A good state is the smallest summary of the world that still lets you predict what happens next and decide what to do.

Think about how humans operate. When you walk across a street, you don't reconstruct every leaf on the tree or the texture of the asphalt. You track a few things: where the cars are, how fast they're moving, whether the light is red. That's a very compressed representation, but it's sufficient for acting in the world. Everything else is, in a sense, noise relative to the task of living and acting.

So the emphasis on minimal information is really about separating what's predictable and relevant from what's unpredictable and irrelevant. If you force a model to account for everything, say by predicting every pixel, it spends enormous capacity on details that don't matter and are often inherently stochastic. The exact way water splashes or how a shadow flickers isn't something you can, or need to, predict precisely. A model that tries too hard ends up blurry, or it overfits to surface statistics instead of learning structure.

There's also a deeper reason related to generalization. The more minimal and abstract your state is, the more likely it captures the causal variables that transfer across situations. If my representation of "a cup on a table" encodes the essential properties, like its position, whether it's full, and whether it's stable, then I can reason about cups I've never seen before. If it encodes the exact lighting and color of one specific cup, that knowledge doesn't transfer.

This connects to a broader debate in our field between generative approaches and more representation-driven approaches. Generative models have been incredibly successful, and I don't think pixel-level modeling is useless. It's a powerful training signal. But I'd argue that the goal shouldn't be the pixels themselves. The pixels are a means to an end. What we ultimately want is a latent space where the state of the world is captured efficiently, where planning and reasoning become tractable.

And "minimal" doesn't mean "impoverished." It's minimal relative to sufficiency. You want everything you need and nothing you don't. Finding that balance is actually one of the hardest open problems. The right level of abstraction depends on the task, the time scale, and the agent. A robot arm grasping an object needs different information from a system planning a route across a city. So I think a big part of the research frontier is figuring out how to learn these representations so that the right kind of minimality emerges, rather than hand-designing it.

So in short, the emphasis on minimal information is about efficiency, robustness, and generalization. It's what lets a model understand the world rather than just memorize its appearance.

r001.rationale: The response says a state should not include every pixel or sensory detail and warns against accounting for everything, but it does not explain that an unconstrained state description could exhaustively specify the environment’s physical parameters.

fable-5.1.text:
The way I think about it is this: state is whatever you need to carry forward so that the past no longer matters. If I have the state, I should be able to predict what happens next without replaying the entire history. So the question becomes, what is the smallest thing that still lets me do that?

In reinforcement learning the classic definition is sufficient statistics. The state is a compression of everything that has happened, and it is sufficient if nothing in the history adds predictive power beyond it. Minimal information is not a stylistic preference, it is the definition. Anything extra is not state, it is just baggage.

Why does this matter so much for us in vision? Because images are the opposite of minimal. A single frame contains millions of pixel values, and almost none of them matter for deciding what to do. The texture of a wall, the exact shade of the sky, these are real information about the world, but they are not information about the state in the sense that affects the agent. If your representation keeps all of it, you have made the learning problem enormously harder for no benefit.

So when I push for minimal information, I am really pushing for a representation that separates what is causally relevant from what is merely present. A good world model is one that has thrown away as much as it can get away with. And it turns out that is also a good test of understanding. If a model can predict the next state from a very compact code, that tells you it has actually figured out the underlying structure rather than memorizing surface appearance.

There is a practical side as well. Smaller state means faster planning, easier generalization, and far less room for spurious correlations to sneak in. When you see models fail on distribution shift, very often it is because they latched onto some irrelevant detail that happened to correlate with the right answer during training. Minimality is a kind of discipline against that.

The hard part, and the honest part, is that we do not know in advance what is minimal. The whole challenge of representation learning is discovering it from data rather than hand designing it. So the emphasis on minimal information is less a recipe and more an objective. It tells you what you are aiming at, even when you are still figuring out how to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says images contain millions of pixel values and that keeping irrelevant visual details makes learning harder, but it does not explain that an unconstrained state description could require exhaustively specifying the environment’s physical parameters.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is: minimal information for what? If you want to predict how an environment will evolve, you don’t necessarily need to preserve every detail of everything you’ve observed. You need the information that makes a difference to what happens next.

For example, imagine a ball moving across a table. Its position alone may not be enough to predict where it will go; you also need its velocity. But the pattern on the table might be irrelevant. So a state is a compact summary of the past that preserves what you need for prediction—and, if you’re acting in the environment, for predicting the consequences of your actions.

The emphasis on minimality is about removing redundancy without losing that predictive information. It doesn’t mean making the representation as small as possible at any cost. If you throw away something essential, you no longer have an adequate description of the state.

r001.rationale: The response says a state need not preserve every observed detail and should remove redundancy, but it does not explain that without a minimal-information constraint one might have to describe the environment’s physical parameters exhaustively.

sol-6.1.text:
The key is that a state should contain enough information to predict what happens next, given an action. You don’t necessarily need the entire history or every detail of the environment. You want to retain the information that matters for that prediction.

For example, if you’re tracking a moving ball, its position alone may not be enough—you also need its velocity. But the color of the ball might be irrelevant. So “minimal” doesn’t mean as little information as possible in an absolute sense. It means a compact representation that still preserves what you need to describe how the environment will evolve.

r001.rationale: The response says a state need not include every detail and gives color as an irrelevant detail, but it does not explain that without the minimal-information constraint, characterizing the state could require exhaustively describing the environment’s physical parameters.
